questions.q: What fertility rate keeps a population stable?
a: About 2.1 children per woman
About 1.5 children per woman
About 3.5 children per woman
About 1.0 child per woman
questions.why: Lesson 1 says countries need women to produce about 2.1 children each to replace both parents and offset early deaths.

a: Countries below 1.5 children rarely climb back above it
Governments that pay for larger families lose elections
Fertility rises once cities become wealthier
Religious groups always have more children than others
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that once fertility falls below 1.5, societies reorganize in ways that discourage births and cannot recover.

questions.q: What does the dependency ratio compare?
a: Working people with retired people they support
Births with deaths in a given year
Urban residents with rural residents
Education spending with healthcare spending
questions.why: Lesson 2 defines the dependency ratio as how many working people there are compared with government-dependent retirees.

questions.q: Why may UN population forecasts be too cautious?
a: Poorer countries are seeing faster fertility declines
They assume fertility will fall even faster than it has
They ignore migration between developed countries
They rely on interviews rather than official statistics
questions.why: Lesson 3 says forecasters assume less-developed countries will follow the old pace, but their fertility is dropping faster and more dramatically.

questions.q: Which cultural loss does depopulation bring?
a: Small languages die as their speakers move and fade
Fewer people means less art is produced worldwide
Traditional foods disappear from wealthy cities
Religious practice declines in every region
questions.why: Lesson 2 notes that the world's languages are dying out as small populations collapse and urbanize into dominant cultures.
